messages.subject: Advertisement for new book on hierarchical models: Applied hierarchical modeling in ecology
parts:
Dear all,

we have now mentioned our new book a couple of times on this list, so let's make it official and formal once and for all.

Our new book Applied hierarchical modeling in ecology (Academic Press, 2016), or AHM for short, provides an up-to-date synthesis on the hierarchical modeling of abundance, occurrence and community metrics such as species richness in what we call "meta-population designs". By the latter, we mean the very common case where you have measured these things at multiple sites. That is, the typical data collection protocol for occupancy and N-mixture models etc. Not surprisingly, one big feature of almost all the models in our book is an explicit model component for measurement error (that is, typically for false-negative errors).

The book is written in a similar style as the legendary "gentle intro to MARK" by Evan Cooch as well as my two earlier books on BUGS for ecologists (Kery, 2010; and Kery & Schaub, 2012). That also means that there are abundant and fully documented code examples, that take you right from the start (e.g., reading data in and formatting them) of an analysis to fitting the model, doing GoF assessments and presenting results, often with the forming of predictions (very important !). We are convinced that ecologists learn statistical modeling best by studying a fully running recipe for an analysis, which they can then take as a template for their own analysis.

We expect this book to be useful for people on this list as well as those on the HMecology list. We fit all models with maximum likelihood (that is, with unmarked) if we can fit them in this way and of course in one of the BUGS engines (in our case, good old WinBUGS and JAGS). For every model type we give an easy intro to the model. As another key feature of our book, we use data simulation to explain a model: showing how you simulate a data set under a model is a very accessible way of describing that model. But of course we also explain each model in equations and in words, and there are some likelihoods around, too.

The book comes in two hefty volumes and we almost feel the need to apologize for that. AHM was originally planned as a single volume, but then we recognized the wealth of material at our hands and our baby grew and so now there will be two volumes. We are almost done with the 2nd round of proofs for volume 1, which is due in mid-November 2016 and will have close to 800 pages (again, sorry for that ;) ....). Volume 2 will be published sometimes later in next year.

There is a book web site under construction which directs you to the Amazon page: www.mbr-pwrc.usgs.gov/pubanalysis/keryroylebook/

Here below is the Table of contents of volume 1 and the planned ToC for volume 2.



Volume 1: Prelude and static models

Preface

 

Part 1: Prelude

1. Distribution, abundance and species richness in ecology

2. What are hierarchical models and how do we analyze them ?

3. Linear models, generalized linear models (GLMs), and random-effects: the components of hierarchical models

4. Introduction to data simulation

5. The Bayesian modeling software BUGS and JAGS

 

Part 2: Models for static systems

6. Modeling abundance using binomial N-mixture models

7. Modeling abundance using multinomial N-mixture models

8. Modeling abundance using hierarchical distance sampling

9. Advanced hierarchical distance sampling

10. Modeling distribution and occurrence using site-occupancy models

11. Community models

 

Volume 2: Dynamic and advanced models

Part 3: Models for dynamic systems

12. Modeling population dynamics with Poisson generalized linear mixed models and extensions

13. Modeling population dynamics with replicate counts within a season

14. Modeling population dynamics with distance sampling data

15. Hierarchical models of survival

16. Modeling species distribution and range dynamics using dynamic occupancy models

17. Modeling metacommunity dynamics using dynamic community models

 

Part 4: Advanced models

18. Multi-state occupancy models

19. Modeling false-positives

20. Models for species interactions

21. Spatial models I (CAR, spatial exponential)

22. Spatial models II (static and dynamic autologistic, IFM)

23. Combination approaches / Integrated models

24. Spatial distance sampling and spatial capture-recapture (SCR)

 

25. Conclusions

______________________________________________________________
 
Marc Kéry

www.vogelwarte.ch
Swiss Ornithological Institute | Seerose 1 | CH-6204 Sempach | Switzerland

Dear all,

we have now mentioned our new book a couple of times on this list, so let's make it official and formal once and for all.

Our new book Applied hierarchical modeling in ecology (Academic Press, 2016), or AHM for short, provides an up-to-date synthesis on the hierarchical modeling of abundance, occurrence and community metrics such as species richness in what we call "meta-population designs". By the latter, we mean the very common case where you have measured these things at multiple sites. That is, the typical data collection protocol for occupancy and N-mixture models etc. Not surprisingly, one big feature of almost all the models in our book is an explicit model component for measurement error (that is, typically for false-negative errors).

The book is written in a similar style as the legendary "gentle intro to MARK" by Evan Cooch as well as my two earlier books on BUGS for ecologists (Kery, 2010; and Kery & Schaub, 2012). That also means that there are abundant and fully documented code examples, that take you right from the start (e.g., reading data in and formatting them) of an analysis to fitting the model, doing GoF assessments and presenting results, often with the forming of predictions (very important !). We are convinced that ecologists learn statistical modeling best by studying a fully running recipe for an analysis, which they can then take as a template for their own analysis.

messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Re: Advertisement for new book on hierarchical models: Applied hierarchical modeling in ecology
parts:
Dear Augusto,

 

I think you must be right and about the AHMbook zip being only for Windows users. We have to see how to format that into a tar to let Linux users enjoy the package.

 

The sim function in chapter 1 is in the R package. For your convenience, it’s repeated down here.

 

Best regards  --- Marc

 

sim.fn <- function (quad.size = 10, cell.size = 1, intensity = 1, show.plot = TRUE)

{

    exp.M <- intensity * quad.size^2

    breaks <- seq(0, quad.size, cell.size)

    n.cell <- (quad.size/cell.size)^2

    mid.pt <- breaks[-length(breaks)] + 0.5 * cell.size

    M <- rpois(1, exp.M)

    u1 <- runif(M, 0, quad.size)

    u2 <- runif(M, 0, quad.size)

    N <- as.matrix(table(cut(u1, breaks = breaks), cut(u2, breaks = breaks)))

    lambda <- round(mean(N), 2)

    var <- var(c(N))

    z <- N

    z[z > 1] <- 1

    psi <- mean(z)

    if (show.plot) {

        par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(5, 5, 5, 2), cex.lab = 1.5,

            cex.axis = 1.3, cex.main = 1.3)

        plot(u1, u2, xlab = "x coord", ylab = "y coord", cex = 1,

            pch = 16, asp = 1, main = paste("Point pattern: \nIntensity =",

                intensity, ", M =", M, "inds."), xlim = c(0,

                quad.size), ylim = c(0, quad.size), frame = F,

            col = "red")

        polygon(c(0, quad.size, quad.size, 0), c(0, 0, quad.size,

            quad.size), lwd = 3, col = NA, border = "black")

        plot(u1, u2, xlab = "x coord", ylab = "y coord", cex = 1,

            pch = 16, asp = 1, main = paste("Abundance pattern: \nRealized mean density =",

                lambda, "\nSpatial variance =", round(var, 2)),

            xlim = c(0, quad.size), ylim = c(0, quad.size), frame = F,

            col = "red")

        for (i in 1:length(breaks)) {

            for (j in 1:length(breaks)) {

                segments(breaks[i], breaks[j], rev(breaks)[i],

                  breaks[j])

                segments(breaks[i], breaks[j], breaks[i], rev(breaks)[j])

            }

        }

        for (i in 1:length(mid.pt)) {

            for (j in 1:length(mid.pt)) {

                text(mid.pt[i], mid.pt[j], N[i, j], cex = 10^(0.8 -

                  0.4 * log10(n.cell)), col = "blue")

            }

        }

        polygon(c(0, quad.size, quad.size, 0), c(0, 0, quad.size,

            quad.size), lwd = 3, col = NA, border = "black")

        plot(u1, u2, xlab = "x coord", ylab = "y coord", cex = 1,

            pch = 16, asp = 1, main = paste("Occurrence pattern: \nRealized occupancy =",

                round(psi, 2)), xlim = c(0, quad.size), ylim = c(0,

                quad.size), frame = F, col = "red")

        for (i in 1:length(breaks)) {

            for (j in 1:length(breaks)) {

                segments(breaks[i], breaks[j], rev(breaks)[i],

                  breaks[j])

                segments(breaks[i], breaks[j], breaks[i], rev(breaks)[j])

            }

        }

        for (i in 1:(length(breaks) - 1)) {

            for (j in 1:(length(breaks) - 1)) {

                polygon(c(breaks[i], breaks[i + 1], breaks[i +

                  1], breaks[i]), c(breaks[j], breaks[j], breaks[j +

                  1], breaks[j + 1]), col = "black", density = z[i,

                  j] * 100)

            }

        }

        polygon(c(0, quad.size, quad.size, 0), c(0, 0, quad.size,

            quad.size), lwd = 3, col = NA, border = "black")

        plot(table(N), xlab = "Abundance (N)", ylab = "Number of cells",

            col = "black", xlim = c(0, max(N)), main = "Frequency of N with mean density (blue)",

            lwd = 3, frame = F)

        abline(v = lambda, lwd = 3, col = "blue")

    }

    return(list(quad.size = quad.size, cell.size = cell.size,

        intensity = intensity, exp.N = exp.M, breaks = breaks,

        n.cell = n.cell, mid.pt = mid.pt, M = M, u1 = u1, u2 = u2,

        N = N, z = z, psi = psi))

}
